facts.claim: "Inside a Bar" was released on February 13, 2024 as the second single from The One & Only Scott H. Biram, ahead of the album's March 29, 2024 release on Bloodshot Records.
Scott H. Biram is credited as the sole writer and composer of "Inside A Bar".

Biram describes the song as a classic country-style drinking song he wrote a couple of years before its release. He says he tried to capture a very slow night at a country dive, with a handful of regulars at closing time.
Biram says he played all the instruments on the entire record. The music video shows him with a band only as a dream sequence.
The video was directed by Biram's friend Frank "Coach" Weysos. The song's narrator is both the lonely bar regular and the frontman playing to nobody on a Monday night.
Biram told PopMatters he was aiming for an old Waylon-era sound, but the song came out like a Johnny Lee-style, Urban Cowboy-type song, with a simple one-four-five structure and no bridge.
Biram said he was going for the sound of loneliness and alcoholism colliding.
Biram used the pandemic shutdown to write, record and produce nine new songs and two traditional covers for The One & Only Scott H. Biram. It is his 13th album overall and 9th for Bloodshot.
Glide Magazine, which premiered the video, called the song a dusty country ballad with twangy guitars. It said the song is split in half by guitar solos that lean toward psychedelia.
Biram nearly died in a head-on collision with a semi truck in 2003. He then recorded the EP Rehabilitation Blues while confined to bed.

research.lineage: The song sits in the Texas outlaw and honky-tonk tradition of Waylon Jennings, Willie Nelson and Dale Watson, filtered through Biram's one-man-band blues, country and punk approach.

draft:
In the video for **Inside A Bar**, the band behind Scott H. Biram only exists in a dream sequence. That fits a song about a man alone in two ways. Biram played every instrument on the record, and the narrator he wrote is both a lonely regular on a stool and the frontman playing to nobody on a Monday night. The person singing and the person not listening are the same guy.

Biram calls it a classic country drinking song, written a couple of years before it came out. He was trying to catch a very slow night at a country dive, a handful of regulars hanging on at closing time. He has also put it more bluntly: he wanted the sound of loneliness and alcoholism colliding. The song doesn't pretend those are separate problems. The empty room is the reason for the next drink, and the next drink keeps the room empty.

The recording sounds like that room. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar keeps a steady pattern, the bass walks underneath, and the drums shuffle along on brushes at a slow, unhurried pace. Electric guitar slides in with bluesy fills between the lines. The mix is dry and close, with no gloss and no harmonies. Nobody comes in to sing along, which is the whole point. The voice is raw and a little strained, closer to talking than performing, like someone who has stopped trying to win over a crowd that was never there.

Biram told PopMatters he was reaching for an old Waylon-era sound, and the song came out more like Johnny Lee and the Urban Cowboy years instead: a simple one-four-five progression, no bridge. That miss works in its favor. Waylon's outlaw records carried a swagger, and this song has none. It sits in the Texas honky-tonk line of Waylon, Willie and Dale Watson, but it comes filtered through the one-man-band approach Biram has built from blues, country and punk. The plain changes keep it humble, a jukebox song about the kind of bar that has a jukebox. Glide Magazine heard the guitar solos that split the song in half leaning toward psychedelia, a brief drift out of the room before the closing-time grind pulls it back.

Biram wrote, recorded and produced the album during the pandemic shutdown, which gives the song's empty dive an echo it may not have had when he wrote it. A man playing every part himself, for no one, during a stretch when no one could gather, was making a song about exactly that.

It sticks because it lets you sit in the quiet after last call, where the loneliness of playing to nobody and the loneliness of drinking alone turn out to be the same feeling.
